Two Hundred People: Reasoning That Travels Without Its Author

Playbooklowob research

By lowob · 14 October 2026 · 7-minute read · Strategy

At a few hundred people, founders make a small fraction of the decisions. Managers make most of them, many managers have never met the people whose decisions they inherit, and turnover becomes constant. The enterprise brain's job becomes delegation: letting good reasoning travel. Four things do that: formal decision classes, a precedent slot before each decision, a standard handover pack, and a first calibration in one high-volume class. The trap is compliance theatre.

This is the fourth rung of The scale ladder. The previous rung, Fifty people: when words start to mean different things, dealt with shared meaning. At two hundred, the problem is delegation.

What delegation breaks

Growth introduces a middle layer. Decisions that a founder once made in a minute, with full context, are now made by a team lead with partial context, often following a precedent set by someone who has since left. The organisation is making more decisions than ever, and each one is made with less of the history behind it.

Turnover makes this routine rather than occasional. The US Bureau of Labor Statistics reported median tenure with the current employer of 4.1 years in January 2026, and 3.9 years in the private sector. In a firm of two hundred, people change roles or leave most months, and every move takes reasons with it. Our piece Handovers are where reasoning pours out describes the mechanism.

The result is inconsistency that nobody sees until someone measures it. Daniel Kahneman and colleagues described the method in Harvard Business Review in October 2016 as a noise audit: several professionals in the same role assess the same cases, and the spread of their answers measures the noise. In one audit at an insurer, as reported by Insurance Thought Leadership, executives expected about a 10% difference between the high and low quotes their 48 underwriters set on the same case. The typical difference was 55%.

This is also the first stage at which some decision classes become frequent enough to learn from. Sales deals, support escalations, hiring decisions and discount approvals each run into the hundreds a year.

The organisation is making more decisions than ever, and each one is made with less of the history behind it.

Decision classes, formally

Define the recurring classes properly now. For each: the owner, the template, the needs list (what a good decision in this class requires), and the falsifier convention. A discount approval should look the same wherever in the company it is made, and be comparable with every other discount approval.

ElementWhat it specifiesExample: discount approval
OwnerWho is accountable for the class and its templateHead of revenue operations
TemplateThe fields every decision in the class recordsDeal size, discount, reason, approver, expected effect
Needs listWhat a good decision must have consideredMargin floor, competitor price evidence, renewal terms
Falsifier conventionHow "this was wrong" is defined, and when it is checkedCustomer churns or downgrades within 12 months
Precedent ruleWhich prior decisions count as comparableSame segment, deal size within 30%, last 18 months

Kahneman's prescription for noise points the same way: where a formula is not feasible, give people procedures that structure their judgment so similar cases are treated alike. A shared template and needs list is that procedure. Our piece on the deal desk shows how one commercial class is usually run at this size.

Precedent for managers

The single most valuable feature at this stage is the precedent slot: before a manager decides, the three most comparable prior decisions in that class, with outcomes. It gives a new team lead the benefit of the decisions their predecessors made, without needing the predecessors.

Precedent only works if decisions in the class were recorded the same way, which is why the classes come first. With a consistent template, finding the three closest prior cases is a straightforward retrieval task. Our explainer What is decision precedent in AI? covers how assistants can surface it, and why the outcome field matters more than the summary.

Handovers become routine

With regular departures and internal moves, handovers happen most months. Make the five-part handover pack standard for any role that owns decisions.

PartWhat it contains
DecisionsThe open and recent decisions the role owns, with reasons and falsifier dates
Open threadsCommitments in progress, with the next action and its date
RelationshipsThe people inside and outside the firm who matter, and the state of each
GraveyardWhat was tried and abandoned, and why, so it is not retried blindly
Question logWhat the outgoing person was asked most, and the answers

It is the cheapest protection against losing reasoning when people move. On the commercial line, the same idea applies to deals moving from sales to delivery, covered in The handover from sales to delivery.

The first calibration

Pick the highest-volume class with outcomes that arrive within two quarters, often sales deals or renewals, and add a probability to each decision. After a year you will know, for the first time, whether the organisation's judgment in that class is well calibrated, and whose calls are reliable.

The forecasting research supports the effort. Barbara Mellers, Philip Tetlock and colleagues, summarising the Good Judgment Project, report that training in probabilistic reasoning helps, that teams forecast significantly better than individuals working alone, and that well-designed aggregation of forecasts beat the simple average by as much as 60%. None of that is possible without a recorded probability and a recorded outcome. Our piece Calibration is the honest learning signal sets out the method.

The trap: compliance theatre

The trap at two hundred is compliance theatre. Templates get longer, fields multiply, and people fill them to satisfy the process rather than to record their thinking. Hold the line on the three-field floor: decision, reason, what would change your mind. Draft the rest. Measure capture time and keep it under a minute.

In practice: define the ten most common decision classes with owner, template, needs list and falsifier convention. Add a precedent slot to the workflow for each class. Make the handover pack mandatory for any role that owns decisions. Start calibration in one high-volume class with short outcome lag. Audit capture time quarterly, and cut any field that is not used.

What would prove this wrong: two-hundred-person organisations without structured decision classes or precedent showing no more inconsistency in similar decisions, and no slower manager ramp-up, than those with them. A noise audit in one class is the cheapest way to find out. The next rung, One thousand people: governance arrives, is where outsiders start asking to see the record.

lowob takeaways

  • Assume inconsistency until measured. Run a small noise audit in one class before arguing about it.
  • Formalise the classes. Owner, template, needs list and falsifier convention for the ten most common.
  • Show precedent before the decision. Three comparable prior cases, with outcomes.
  • Standardise handovers. Decisions, open threads, relationships, graveyard and question log.
  • Guard the floor. Three required fields, everything else drafted, capture under a minute.

Common questions

How do growing companies keep decisions consistent as managers change?

Define recurring decision classes formally and add a precedent slot that shows the three most comparable prior decisions, with outcomes, before a manager decides.

What should a handover pack include?

Five parts: decisions, open threads, relationships, graveyard and question log. It should be standard for any role that owns decisions.

What is a noise audit?

A test in which several people in the same role assess the same cases independently. The spread of their answers measures inconsistency, which is usually much larger than leaders expect.

How do you stop decision templates becoming bureaucratic?

Hold a three-field floor: decision, reason and what would change your mind. Draft the rest, keep capture under a minute, and cut fields nobody uses.
